item.title: Stochastic Shockwave Dynamics in First-Order Traffic Flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.23022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Moving congestion fronts vary across realizations even when the traffic-flow law is fixed. This paper develops a generator-based formulation of the Lighthill--Whitham--Richards (LWR) model with random initial density and a deterministic fundamental diagram. Randomness enters through the initial spatial density field; every realization follows the same conservation law. For a smooth strictly concave fundamental diagram, we adapt established one-sided spatial Markov closure to traffic variables under the stated spatial-process and regularity assumptions, and derive a kinetic balance for physically normalized front intensities. Evolving the spatial generator provides density laws and congestion-front statistics without solving a road-grid problem for every realization. The formulation is continuous in physical space and time, while its numerical implementation approximates density state and integrates physical time. Four experiments distinguish deterministic consistency from stochastic comparison. Riemann and signal examples recover independently constructed exact LWR solutions. Smooth strictly concave approximations approach the deterministic triangular-diagram signal solution over the tested finite horizons; this does not establish stochastic closure at contacts or the capacity kink. A matched Monte Carlo Godunov ensemble evaluates front counts, sizes, mergers, and density distributions. The evolved generator also yields an instantaneous travel-time distribution for a frozen density field, compared with the same functional of the matched Godunov profiles. This quantity is not experienced travel time through evolving traffic. Resolution checks identify remaining normalization and small-front-loss effects. The contribution is direct evolution and interpretation of traffic-state and front distributions under a fixed first-order traffic law.
item.dc:creator: Yanlin Zhang, Alireza Talebpour

item.title: Stationary analysis of adaptive aspiration dynamics in graph-structured games
item.description: arXiv:2610.23418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aspiration dynamics can favor cooperation on finite graphs through a purely local satisfaction mechanism. In the model studied here, individuals compare their payoffs with adaptive aspiration levels and revise their strategies through a self-switching Fermi rule. Although the aspirations are continuous and endogenous, the resulting finite-population process has a unique stationary distribution for every finite selection intensity and every finite connected graph under degree-normalized average payoffs when restricted to the compact forward-invariant state space in which aspirations lie in the payoff interval. In the weak-selection regime, the first-order stationary abundance shift is positive when \(R+S>T+P\), negative when \(R+S<T+P\), and zero when \(R+S=T+P\). In the equality case, higher-order terms may determine its direction. The condition \(R+S>T+P\) means that, under neutrality, the expected payoff of a cooperator exceeds that of a defector. The stationary variance reveals a different effect whose first-order correction is governed by the payoff-range contrast \((R-S)-(T-P)\). This contrast compares how strongly cooperator and defector payoffs respond to changes in local neighborhood composition and therefore measures the relative sensitivity of their payoffs to the local environment. Under degree-normalized average payoffs, these first-order results hold on every finite connected graph and are independent of degree sequence, topology, and aspiration learning rate. Simulations on regular and heterogeneous graphs compare averaged and accumulated payoffs and illustrate that graph heterogeneity and the aspiration learning rate can affect stationary behavior away from weak selection. The first-order coefficients are derived from the finite stochastic process and do not use pair approximation, mean-field closure, or a large-population limit.
item.dc:creator: Dhaker Kroumi

item.title: Two Seconds per Day: Limitations of Circadian Burden Metrics in the Permanent Daylight Saving Time Debate
item.description: arXiv:2610.23688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A 1410-word Letter to the Editor reporting a bug in a study published in PNAS. The authors of the original study executed their code to compute the yearly circadian burden with an Earth rotating backwards: the sun rising in the West, setting on the East. The authors have acknowledged the error and re-executed the code. We analyze authors's new average yearly circadian burden in the US to show that these results do not provide significant information for the current debate on the time policy.
item.dc:creator: Jos\'e Mar\'ia Mart\'in-Olalla, Jorge Mira

item.title: Emergent Discrimination and Polarization in Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.22701v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study theoretically how discrimination and polarization can emerge in a population of learning agents. Each agent uses an adaptive linear decision layer to map a language-model embedding of an issue to a binary opinion and maintains an evolving estimate of how much it trusts every other agent. Through pairwise interactions, agents update both their decision weights and trust estimates using an online Bayesian rule derived from teacher-student learning over a noisy channel. In-context-learning experiments with large language models qualitatively reproduce the predicted opinion and trust updates. We then assign each agent one of two arbitrary group labels, A or B, and model group bias by allowing a fraction $f_b$ of agents to shift its perceived agreement with each message by a strength $b$, a bias steering prejudice, depending on whether the sender and receiver share a label. We use order parameters from statistical mechanics to connect these local dynamics to collective states and transitions. Starting from uniformly random initial conditions, simulations reveal a rich phase diagram in the $(b,f_b)$ plane, comprising four collective states: spin-glass frustrated out-group favoritism, nondiscriminatory polarization, discrimination with opinion alignment, and discrimination without opinion alignment. Which state emerges depends on both the strength and prevalence of the bias. These results show how simple local learning dynamics can generate qualitatively distinct forms of polarization and discrimination, underscoring the need for population-level safety analysis of multi-agent systems. They also suggest measurable order parameters for characterizing analogous collective states in human societies.
item.dc:creator: Nestor Caticha, Jo\~ao Henrique Sant'Ana, Felippe Alves, Davi Bastos Costa, Mariana Mercucci, Juan P. Neirotti, Otavio Citton, Renato Vicente

item.title: Validating LLM-generated political networks with survey-reported partisan exposure
item.description: arXiv:2610.23199v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior in social science research, including decisions, interactions, and social relationships. However, in network formation tasks, existing evaluations often focus on aggregate network properties, while networks with plausible structural properties may still fail to reproduce individuals' social and political environments. Here, we generate LLM-based political networks using personas sampled from the nationally representative ANES 2020--2022 Social Media Study and use respondents' survey-reported partisan exposure as an empirical benchmark for the political environments generated for the corresponding personas. We first characterize the structural properties and political assortativity of the generated networks, and then compare ego-level partisan exposure with the survey. We find that the structure and political assortativity of the generated networks vary across experimental configurations. More importantly, when comparing generated partisan exposure with the survey, some models generate stronger separation between Democratic and Republican egos than reported in the survey, with higher same-party and lower cross-party exposure, while others mainly underestimate Republican exposure across ego groups. Moreover, networks with similar political assortativity can still generate different partisan environments around the same personas, including among networks with plausible structural properties. Finally, generated networks show group-specific errors, under- or overestimating exposure to either Democrats or Republicans for specific social groups. These findings show that evaluating LLM-based social simulations only through aggregate outcomes can hide errors in the local environments through which those outcomes emerge, highlighting the importance of validation at both aggregate and individual levels.
item.dc:creator: Marco Tonin, Michele Tizzoni, Bruno Lepri, Luca Maria Aiello

item.title: Bridging the Language Gap in Scholarly Data II: Enhancing Gender Inference for Chinese Names
item.description: arXiv:2610.23734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Perceived gender inference from names is important for inclusive scientometrics research, yet existing methods perform poorly on non-Western scholars. We address this gap for Chinese names, which appear in two forms, Hanzi and Pinyin, its Romanized form (e.g., Zhang Wei, Li Na). In international bibliographic records, names are often available only in Pinyin. However, a single pinyin name can correspond to multiple distinct hanzi characters with different gender associations, so gender inference from Pinyin alone is intrinsically ambiguous. To address this, we first develop two hanzi models, a regression model that produces a continuous gender score from 0 (male) to 1 (female), and a classification model that outputs one of three labels (\em{male}, \em{neutral}, \em{female}). We train them on a sample of hanzi names from Chinese-language physics publications, rated by 11 native Chinese speakers. On this sample, the models achieve an RMSE of $0.09$ and an R$^2$ of $0.85$ (regression), and macro-AUC of $0.97$ and a Cohen's $\kappa$ of $0.81$ (classification), demonstrating high performance that is robust to class imbalance. For pinyin names, we propose a pipeline that aggregates hanzi predictions via transliteration and frequency weighting, together with an ambiguity score that flags names whose gender cannot be resolved from Pinyin alone. Benchmarked against three off-the-shelf tools (Namsor, GPT, and Claude), our models achieve the highest agreement with human annotations for both gender scores and gender labels, in both scripts. Applied to an independent sample of Chinese-named authors in APS journals, our models assign a gender to every name, whereas existing Pinyin-based methods leave between 20\% and 100\% of names unclassified. These findings demonstrate the importance of hanzi-level information for reliable gender inference of Chinese names. Code and data are publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Lisette Esp\'in-Noboa, Mingrong She, Ana Maria Jaramillo, Liuhuaying Yang

item.title: Predictability of Human Movements across Industry Sectors using Multilayer Networks
item.description: arXiv:2607.28494v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting the patterns of human movement is important to applications from urban design to disease control and emergency response. In this work, we leverage machine learning (ML) to study the predictability of movements to different types of locations (e.g., movements to grocery stores, to schools, or to hospitals). Our approach relies on developing multilayer mobility networks encoding movements between census tracts with network layers associated with different industry sectors. We study the predictability of node degrees across layers, studying which industries are easier/harder to predict. Rather than treat prediction as an end in itself, we propose ML predictability as an exploratory tool to understand multilayer network organization. Our results suggest that node's out-degrees are easy to predict, since they are driven by census tract populations; whereas in-degrees are harder to predict, since persons can be drawn to diverse type of locations in a census tract. We also find that movements to certain industry types (e.g., restaurants) are easier to predict than others, and the different industrie's predictability are positively correlated with the number of movements to those types of locations. These findings provide a practical step toward using ML for multilayer mobility modeling and the many downstream application.
item.dc:creator: Maisha Islam Sejunti, Melissa Butler, Yingjie Hu, Dane Taylor

item.title: Viral mutation spread controlled by inter-host network dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2502.18472v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The increase in the connectivity between hosts in recent times has facilitated the emergence of more aggressive mutant viral strains, making their containment and eradication significantly more challenging compared to the original variants. We focus on the evolution of a new more aggressive mutant strain that appears in the system and competes with a previous version. The role of host interaction network topology in the emergence and spatial diffusion of these highly contagious strains is analyzed, as well as how network-based interventions can help mitigate their spread. To address these issues, we present simplified mathematical models that qualitatively describe the occurrence, propagation, and impact of such mutations within host-interaction networks. By incorporating the topology of the host network into the analysis, a more advanced framework is proposed to curb the growth of mutant strains. Extensive numerical simulations of these models offer insights into the mechanisms driving viral evolution, the dynamics of contagion, and the topological influence of host networks on viral spread and containment strategies.
item.dc:creator: Javier L\'opez-Pedrares, M. Elena V\'azquez-Cend\'on, Alberto P. Mu\~nuzuri

item.title: Six objects reported at 480 mph in a declassified military infrared video show brightness flicker at bird wingbeat rates
item.description: arXiv:2610.08692v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In September 2026 the U.S. Department of War released an infrared video recorded from a military aircraft over the Middle East, with a mission report describing six small spherical objects moving at an estimated 480 miles per hour. We measure the brightness of each object in every frame. All six brighten and dim steadily at 7.1-7.9 times per second, each at its own rate and out of step with the others. Tests with planted constant-brightness objects show that neither compression nor the sensor produces this flicker. The same analysis, applied to the Galileo Project's ground-based infrared cameras near Las Vegas, finds flying animals beating steadily at 3.4-10.0 times per second, within the range of bird wingbeats. A nearly stationary object at 60-80% of the aircraft's height would produce the reported ground-projected speed of 480 miles per hour. The six objects are best explained as a small flock of birds flying nearer to the aircraft than the crew assumed. The same analysis also finds 19 objects with similar beats, at 2.3-11.0 times per second, in nine other released military videos. Releasing the redacted sensor and platform data would provide information that could refute the bird hypothesis
item.dc:creator: Jacob Haqq-Misra, Ravi Kopparapu, Richard Cloete, Omer Eldadi, Michael Shermer, Abraham Loeb
